results.description: Calculate aggregate for US construction — quantity, material and cost with waste, in US customary and metric units.

schemas.name: Calculator Street
schemas.description: Calculate aggregate for US construction — quantity, material and cost with waste, in US customary and metric units.

mainEntity.name: What does the Aggregate Calculator calculate?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Aggregate Calculator estimates aggregate quantity for US jobs — Cubic yards and cubic feet, Tons and pounds using 1.35–1.60 t/yd³, Cost per ton or per yard with waste. Enter dimensions, choose units, add waste and price to get instant results.

mainEntity.name: How do I measure for aggregate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Measure aggregate 20 ft x 10 ft x 4 in on site. Use the unit selectors — the tool converts inches→feet (÷12) and yards→feet (×3) before math. For non-rectangular, split into rectangles and add.

mainEntity.name: How much waste should I add?

acceptedAnswer.text: Open-graded stone settles ~8% (×1.10), crusher run compacts 15–25% (×1.20). Add after volume.

mainEntity.name: How accurate is this aggregate estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Math is exact for your inputs. Actual needs vary by site, material and installation. Add 5–10% waste for rectangular, 10–15% for irregular.

acceptedAnswer.text: The Brick Waste Calculator estimates brick waste quantity for US jobs — Bricks or blocks per wall area, Mortar volume with 3/8 in joint, Waste-adjusted count and cost. Enter dimensions, choose units, add waste and price to get instant results.

mainEntity.name: How do I measure for brick waste?

acceptedAnswer.text: Measure wall 20 ft x 8 ft, brick 7.5x2.25 in, joint 0.375 in on site. Use the unit selectors — the tool converts inches→feet (÷12) and yards→feet (×3) before math. For non-rectangular, split into rectangles and add.

mainEntity.name: How much waste should I add?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add 7% for cuts and breakage — 10% for arches or curves.

mainEntity.name: How accurate is this brick waste estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Math is exact for your inputs. Actual needs vary by site, material and installation. Add 5–10% waste for rectangular, 10–15% for irregular.

results.description: Calculate concrete for slabs in cubic yards and bags. Enter length, width & thickness to get square feet, yards, 80/60/40lb bags, waste & cost instantly.

schemas.name: Calculator Street
schemas.description: Calculate concrete for slabs in cubic yards and bags. Enter length, width & thickness to get square feet, yards, 80/60/40lb bags, waste & cost instantly.

schemas.name: Concrete Slab Calculator — Yards, Bags & Cost (2026)
schemas.description: Calculate concrete for slabs in cubic yards and bags. Enter length, width & thickness to get square feet, yards, 80/60/40lb bags, waste & cost instantly.

mainEntity.name: How much concrete do I need for a slab?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply length × width × thickness (all in feet) and divide by 27 for cubic yards. Example: 10×10 ft at 4 inches (0.333 ft) = 33.3 ft³ = 1.23 yd³. Add 5–10% for waste and uneven subgrade, then use the calculator — it handles inches-to-feet and shows both yards and bags. For a base layer, add gravel via the Gravel Calculator.

mainEntity.name: How many 80-lb bags are in a yard of concrete?

acceptedAnswer.text: About 45 bags of 80-lb (0.60 ft³ each), 60 bags of 60-lb (0.45 ft³), or 90 bags of 40-lb (0.30 ft³) make one cubic yard (27 ft³). For a 10×10 ft slab at 4 inches you need about 56 bags of 80-lb (1.23 yd³ × 45). The calculator rounds up — you can’t buy part of a bag.

mainEntity.name: How thick should a concrete slab be?

acceptedAnswer.text: Patios, walkways and shed pads: 3.5–4 inches. Driveways, garage floors and RV pads: 5–6 inches, often 4,000 psi mix. Sidewalks: 4 inches. Commercial: 6–8 inches. Thicker adds volume fast — a 6-inch slab uses 50% more than a 4-inch over the same footprint. Confirm with local code and your engineer for loads.

mainEntity.name: Should I order ready-mix or bags?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under ~0.75 yd³ (about 30–40 bags of 80-lb) bags can be practical. Over ~1–1.5 yd³, ready-mix delivery is usually cheaper and far faster. A 12×10 ft patio at 4 inches is 1.48 yd³ — that’s 74 bags of 80-lb with waste, so a truck wins. The calculator shows both so you can compare instantly.

mainEntity.name: How much extra concrete should I order for waste?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add 5–10% for spillage, over-excavation and slight thickness variation — 10% is safe for most residential forms. Keep the subgrade well-compacted and evenly graded to the right depth, and keep an extra bag per 10 as a buffer. The calculator applies waste after volume, then rounds bags up.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate concrete for multiple slabs or an L-shape?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use Number of slabs for identical rectangles, or run the calculator twice for different sizes and sum the waste-adjusted yards. For an L-shape, split it into two rectangles (e.g., 12×10 plus 8×6) and add the cubic yards. Coverage per bag already assumes proper water ratio — don’t thin the mix to stretch it.

mainEntity.name: How much does a concrete slab cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ready-mix is often $140–$180 per yard plus $100–$200 delivery/minimum in 2026; bags are $4–$7 per 80-lb. A 10×10 ft 4-inch slab (~1.35 yd³ with waste) is roughly $200–$300 in ready-mix versus $280–$380 in bags before tax. Enter your price per yard or per bag — the calculator multiplies waste-adjusted yards or the rounded bag count for a material-only total.

schemas.name: Concrete Weight Calculator — Pounds, Tons & Yards (150 lb/ft³)
schemas.description: Calculate concrete weight in pounds, short tons and metric tonnes from length, width and depth. Normal-weight 150 lb/ft³ (4050 lb/yd³) — see weight per sq ft, total weight and truck loads with waste.

mainEntity.name: How much does one cubic yard of concrete weigh?

acceptedAnswer.text: Normal-weight concrete is about 4050 lb per cubic yard (150 lb/ft³ × 27). That's 2.025 short tons or 1.84 metric tonnes. Lightweight is ~2970 lb/yd³ (110 pcf) and cellular ~2430 lb/yd³ (90 pcf). Use 4050 for quick checks: tons = yards × 2.025.

mainEntity.name: How much does a 4-inch, 5-inch or 6-inch slab weigh per square foot?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply thickness (ft) × 150. So 4 in (0.333 ft) = 50 lb/ft², 5 in (0.417 ft) = 62.5 lb/ft², 6 in (0.50 ft) = 75 lb/ft². A 10×12 ft slab 6 in thick is 120 ft² × 75 = 9,000 lb (4.5 tons) — see the worked example on this page. Add rebar ~3–5 lb/ft² for heavy mats.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert cubic yards to tons (or tons back to yards)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tons = Yards × 2.025 (short tons) or Yards × 1.837 (tonnes). Example: 2.22 yd³ × 2.025 = 4.50 tons. Reverse: Yards = Tons ÷ 2.025. Quick rule: 1 ton ≈ 0.493 yd³ of normal concrete. The calculator shows all three at once.

mainEntity.name: How many concrete trucks do I need by weight?

acceptedAnswer.text: By yards: trucks = ceil(yards ÷ 10) — most mixers carry 9–11 yd³. By weight: stay under ~24 tons of concrete per truck plus truck weight to stay under 80,000 lb GVW. A 2.44 yd³, 4.95-ton pour like the example fits in one truck either way.

mainEntity.name: Does rebar change the weight?

acceptedAnswer.text: A little. Heavy rebar adds ~6–8 lb per cubic foot of concrete (≈4–5%). For a footing with #5 @12 in o.c., add 5% to be safe. Light wire mesh is negligible. If your engineer calls out #6 mats, set waste to 15% to cover it.

mainEntity.name: Why does the calculator ask for density?

acceptedAnswer.text: Different mixes weigh different amounts. Normal 4000-psi is 150 pcf; lightweight structural (for decks or roof) is 110–120 pcf and costs more per yard but saves dead load. Always use the density on your mix design — if unsure, keep 150.

schemas.name: Calculator Street
schemas.description: Calculate crawl space for US construction — quantity, material and cost with waste, in US customary and metric units.

mainEntity.name: What does the Crawl Space Calculator calculate?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Crawl Space Calculator estimates crawl space quantity for US jobs — Footing volume in cubic yards, Foundation wall area and concrete, Excavation volume with waste. Enter dimensions, choose units, add waste and price to get instant results.

mainEntity.name: How do I measure for crawl space?

acceptedAnswer.text: Measure crawl space 20 ft x 10 ft x 4 in on site. Use the unit selectors — the tool converts inches→feet (÷12) and yards→feet (×3) before math. For non-rectangular, split into rectangles and add.

mainEntity.name: How much waste should I add?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add 10% for over-excavation and slough — trench sides cave.

mainEntity.name: How accurate is this crawl space estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Math is exact for your inputs. Actual needs vary by site, material and installation. Add 5–10% waste for rectangular, 10–15% for irregular.

schemas.description: Calculate crushed stone for US construction — quantity, material and cost with waste, in US customary and metric units.

mainEntity.name: What does the Crushed Stone Calculator calculate?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Crushed Stone Calculator estimates crushed stone quantity for US jobs — Cubic yards and cubic feet, Tons and pounds using 1.35–1.60 t/yd³, Cost per ton or per yard with waste. Enter dimensions, choose units, add waste and price to get instant results.

mainEntity.name: How do I measure for crushed stone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Measure crushed stone 20 ft x 10 ft x 4 in on site. Use the unit selectors — the tool converts inches→feet (÷12) and yards→feet (×3) before math. For non-rectangular, split into rectangles and add.

mainEntity.name: How much waste should I add?

acceptedAnswer.text: Open-graded stone settles ~8% (×1.10), crusher run compacts 15–25% (×1.20). Add after volume.

mainEntity.name: How accurate is this crushed stone estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Math is exact for your inputs. Actual needs vary by site, material and installation. Add 5–10% waste for rectangular, 10–15% for irregular.

results.title: Deck Material Calculator — Boards, Joists & Cost (2026)
results.description: Calculate deck material — boards, joists & fasteners. Enter deck size, board size, gap & joist spacing — get boards, linear feet & cost.

schemas.name: Calculator Street
schemas.description: Calculate deck material — boards, joists & fasteners. Enter deck size, board size, gap & joist spacing — get boards, linear feet & cost.

schemas.name: Deck Material Calculator — Boards, Joists & Cost (2026)
schemas.description: Calculate deck material — boards, joists & fasteners. Enter deck size, board size, gap & joist spacing — get boards, linear feet & cost.

mainEntity.name: How many deck boards do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rows = Deck width ÷ (board width + gap), then boards = rows × ceil(deck length ÷ board length). Example: 16×12 ft deck with 5.5-inch boards, 0.125-inch gap and 16-ft boards needs 26 boards, 29 with 10% waste. The gap matters — 1/8 vs 1/4 inch changes row count by one or two boards across the width.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate deck square footage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply length × width for square footage — e.g., 16 × 12 = 192 sq ft. Square footage drives board count only indirectly; the real driver is board width plus gap. For a ground-level patio alternative, compare to the Paver Calculator which uses area ÷ paver area.

mainEntity.name: How much decking material do I need including waste?

acceptedAnswer.text: Calculate boards as above, then add waste: 10% for simple rectangles, 15% for diagonal, herringbone or picture-frame borders where cuts increase. Linear feet is boards × board length. The calculator shows both and lets you price per board or per linear foot so you can compare a per-board quote to a per-foot one.

mainEntity.name: How far apart should deck boards be spaced?

acceptedAnswer.text: Typical gap is 1/8 inch (3 mm) for wood and 3/16 inch (4.5 mm) for composite to allow drainage and expansion. Composite manufacturers often specify 1/8–1/4 inch. Too tight traps debris and water; too wide feels uneven. Enter your actual gap — the calculator adds it to board width before dividing the deck width.

mainEntity.name: How many joists do I need and what spacing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Joists = ceil(length ÷ spacing) + 1. Spacing is on-center: 16 inches for 5/4 decking (most common), 12 inches for diagonal decking or many composites, 24 inches only for 2×6 decking. A 16-ft deck at 16-inch spacing needs 13 joists (ledger + rim included; add one for free-standing). Check span tables for your joist size.

mainEntity.name: How many fasteners or hidden clips do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rough rule: 2 fasteners per joist per board. Hidden clips are similar — one clip per joist per board. For 26 boards × 13 joists that’s 676 fasteners. The calculator estimates this so you can order boxes (often 100 or 350 count). Verify with your clip manufacturer — some systems use one clip per board per joist plus starter clips.

mainEntity.name: How much does deck material cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: In 2026, pressure-treated pine is often $2–$4 per linear foot, composite $4–$8, hardwoods higher. Enter your price per board or per linear foot — e.g., $35 per 16-ft board at 29 boards with waste is about $1,015 before tax, joists and fasteners. Compare to a Concrete Slab Calculator patio if you’re deciding between deck and slab.

schemas.name: Calculator Street
schemas.description: Calculate driveway gravel in cubic yards and tons. Enter length, width, depth & layers — get yards, tons & cost with waste for base & top.

schemas.name: Driveway Gravel Calculator — Yards, Tons & Cost (2026)
schemas.description: Calculate driveway gravel in cubic yards and tons. Enter length, width, depth & layers — get yards, tons & cost with waste for base & top.

mainEntity.name: How much gravel do I need for a driveway?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 12×40 ft single-car drive at 6 inches needs about 8.9 yd³ (≈12–13 tons) before waste; a 12×100 ft rural drive at 8 inches needs ~37 yd³ (≈53 tons). Enter your exact length, width and depth, set layers for a two-course build, and the calculator shows both cubic yards and tons — then divide tons by truck capacity (often 12–15 tons per load) to get trips.

mainEntity.name: How deep should a gravel driveway be?

acceptedAnswer.text: New residential: 8 inches total is the safest minimum — 6 inches of compacted crusher-run base plus 2 inches of #57 top. Firm sandy soil with light cars can do 4 inches base + 2 inches top (6 inches total). Soft clay or heavy trucks need 8 inches base + 2–3 inches top (10–11 inches). Resurfacing an existing base needs only 2–3 inches of fresh top stone.

mainEntity.name: What gravel is best for driveways?

acceptedAnswer.text: Crusher run / road base (1.45 t/yd³) for the base — it locks when compacted. #57 crushed stone (1.40 t/yd³) for the surface — drains well and stays put. Avoid rounded pea gravel for the driving surface; it shifts. For decorative borders, size those separately with the Gravel Calculator.

mainEntity.name: How many tons of gravel for a 100-foot driveway?

acceptedAnswer.text: About 42 tons total for a 12×100 ft drive with a standard two-layer build (6-inch base + 2-inch top). That’s roughly 29 yd³ base (41.9 tons) plus 8.5 yd³ surface (11.9 tons). The calculator splits layers so you can order base and surface as separate tickets — never mix them.

mainEntity.name: How do layers and compaction work?

acceptedAnswer.text: Order loose, place compacted. Open-graded #57 settles ~8% (×1.10), dense-graded crusher run compacts 15–25% (×1.20–1.25). The calculator first does Length × Width × Depth ÷ 324 per layer for raw yards, then applies compaction if you’re building a base. Waste (5–10% for a full build) is separate — add it after compaction.

mainEntity.name: How much does driveway gravel cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Material in 2026 is typically $15–$30/ton for crusher run, $28–$45/ton for #57, plus $50–$150 delivery per load. A 12×40 ft two-layer drive is often $600–$1,200 in stone alone before grading or fabric. Enter your price per yard or per ton — the calculator multiplies the waste-adjusted tons or yards so you can compare a per-ton bulk quote to a per-yard bag quote.

mainEntity.name: How do I handle multiple sections or a turnaround?

acceptedAnswer.text: Set Layers to the number of identical rectangles (e.g., 2 for a main run plus a 30×30 ft turnaround as a second area). For different sizes, run the calculator once per section and sum the waste-adjusted tons — or use the Gravel Calculator for each pad and add them. Keep waste at 10% on the total, not per section.

schemas.name: Fence Cost Calculator — Posts, Panels & Gates (2026)
schemas.description: Calculate fence cost — posts, panels, pickets & gates. Enter length, height, spacing & rails to get posts, panels, area & cost for wood, vinyl & chain link.

mainEntity.name: How much does a fence cost per linear foot in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: Installed: chain link $10–$25, pressure-treated wood $15–$30, vinyl $25–$40, composite $30–$50, wrought iron $30–$70 per linear foot at 6 ft height. Material-only is roughly $5–$12 for chain link, $8–$15 for wood, $12–$22 for vinyl. A 150 ft wood privacy fence is often $4,500–$6,800 installed. The calculator shows material-only with waste — get 2–3 local bids for labor, which is ~60% of installed cost.

mainEntity.name: How many fence posts do I need and how far apart?

acceptedAnswer.text: Posts = ceil(effective length ÷ spacing) + 1 + 2 × gates. Spacing is center-to-center: 8 ft is standard for wood and chain link, 6 ft for vinyl. Effective length subtracts gate widths. Example: 100 ft with 8-ft spacing and one 4-ft gate → ceil(96 ÷ 8) + 1 + 2 = 15 posts. Add waste after.

mainEntity.name: What affects fence cost the most?

acceptedAnswer.text: Material choice (3–8× range), fence height (4 ft ×0.75, 8 ft ×1.30 vs 6 ft baseline), post depth and concrete (36-inch holes, ~1.5 ft³ or ~3 bags of 60-lb per post), gate count ($200–$600 walk-through, $300–$1,200 double), and terrain (slope adds $3–$10/ft, clearing $2–$6/ft). Region matters — coastal labor is 30% higher.

mainEntity.name: How much does a fence gate add to the cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Walk-through gates $200–$600 each, double-drive $300–$1,200, automatic $1,900–$6,000+. Each gate also needs two extra posts and hardware. The calculator adds 2 posts per gate and includes gate width in effective length so you can compare a single 4-ft gate vs two gates directly.

mainEntity.name: Wood vs vinyl vs chain link — which should I choose?

acceptedAnswer.text: Chain link: cheapest, 15–20 yr, minimal privacy. Wood (PT pine $8–$15 materials, cedar $15–$25): 15–25 yr with staining every 2–3 years. Vinyl ($12–$22 materials): 25–40 yr, zero maintenance, limited colors and brittle in extreme cold. For a deck perimeter, vinyl or composite often pairs best with composite decking for lifetime cost.

mainEntity.name: How much concrete do I need per post?

acceptedAnswer.text: About 1.5 ft³ per 36-inch hole (4×4 post) — roughly three 60-lb bags (0.45 ft³ each) or two 80-lb bags. Deeper or wider holes on slopes or tall fences (8 ft needs 36-inch depth, 3 bags) use more. The calculator estimates posts × 0.5 bags of 50-lb as a planning figure — confirm with your post-hole depth and bag yield (80-lb = 0.60 ft³, 60-lb = 0.45 ft³).

mainEntity.name: How much waste should I add for a fence?

acceptedAnswer.text: 10% is typical for simple runs on flat ground. Use 15% for sloped, staggered board, or board-on-board designs where cuts increase. Chain link waste is lower (5%). The calculator’s waste multiplies posts, panels and linear rails together — material-only cost then reflects waste-adjusted quantities.

acceptedAnswer.text: The Floor Joist Calculator estimates floor joist quantity for US jobs — Stud count from spacing, Board feet (T x W x L /12), Joist/beam loads with waste. Enter dimensions, choose units, add waste and price to get instant results.

mainEntity.name: How do I measure for floor joist?

acceptedAnswer.text: Measure wall 20 ft, studs 16 in oc on site. Use the unit selectors — the tool converts inches→feet (÷12) and yards→feet (×3) before math. For non-rectangular, split into rectangles and add.

mainEntity.name: How much waste should I add?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add 10% for cuts and cripples — 15% for gable walls.

mainEntity.name: How accurate is this floor joist estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Math is exact for your inputs. Actual needs vary by site, material and installation. Add 5–10% waste for rectangular, 10–15% for irregular.

schemas.description: Calculate gravel in cubic yards and tons for patios, driveways & landscaping. Enter length, width, depth & material — get yards, tons & cost with waste.

schemas.name: Gravel Calculator — Cubic Yards, Tons & Cost (2026)
schemas.description: Calculate gravel in cubic yards and tons for patios, driveways & landscaping. Enter length, width, depth & material — get yards, tons & cost with waste.

mainEntity.name: How much gravel do I need for my project?

acceptedAnswer.text: Measure your area’s length and width, decide on depth, then use the calculator. For a rectangular patio, we convert everything to feet (inches ÷ 12, yards × 3), compute Length × Width × Depth, divide by 27 for cubic yards, then multiply by the material’s density to get tons. Try the Pea Gravel Calculator if you’re using pea gravel specifically, or the Driveway Gravel Calculator for layered driveways.

mainEntity.name: How many tons are in a cubic yard of gravel?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the stone. Most washed gravel is 1.30–1.42 tons per cubic yard: pea gravel ~1.35 t/yd³, crushed stone ~1.40 t/yd³, limestone ~1.60 t/yd³ and granite ~1.42 t/yd³. One cubic yard of pea gravel is about 2,700 lb. Always confirm your yard’s scale weight — wet or dense-graded base can be 10–20% heavier.

mainEntity.name: How deep should gravel be for a patio vs a driveway?

acceptedAnswer.text: Garden paths and patios do well at 2–3 inches (5–7.5 cm) of clean gravel over fabric and a firm base. Residential driveways need 4–6 inches total, usually as a compacted base plus a top course. For a two-layer driveway, use the Driveway Gravel Calculator to size each lift separately and add compaction.

mainEntity.name: How much area does one ton of gravel cover?

acceptedAnswer.text: At 3 inches deep, one ton covers roughly 65–80 sq ft depending on density: limestone ~67 ft², crushed stone ~77 ft², pea gravel ~80 ft², river rock ~81 ft² per ton. Coverage halves if you double depth to 6 inches. The reference table on this page shows tons/yd³ and lb/ft³ so you can plan coverage without re-measuring.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert cubic yards of gravel to tons?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply cubic yards by the density in tons per yard. Example: 2.47 yd³ of pea gravel at 1.35 t/yd³ = 3.33 tons; at $48 per yd³ vs $65 per ton, you can compare quotes. Our calculator shows both units at once so you can order in whichever unit your supplier sells by — tons for bulk, yards for bag comparison.

mainEntity.name: Should I add waste and does gravel compact?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Add 5–10% waste for rectangular areas and 10–15% for curves, slopes or uneven subgrade. Clean open-graded stone (#57, pea gravel) settles about 8% (use 1.10×), while dense-graded crusher run can compact 15–25% (use 1.20× per TxDOT). Decorative rounded stone like pea and river rock does not compact — use 1.00×. The calculator’s waste control is separate from compaction.

mainEntity.name: How much does gravel cost per ton or per yard?

acceptedAnswer.text: In 2026 most bulk gravel is $25–$60 per ton or $40–$75 per cubic yard before delivery, which is often $50–$150 per load or $10–$25 per ton. Price varies by material (limestone and granite cost more than #57) and by region. Enter your local price per yd³ or per ton — the calculator multiplies the waste-adjusted quantity to give a material-only estimate. Labor and delivery are extra.

step.name: Measure area
step.text: Measure length, width and depth of your project area in feet or inches.

step.name: Enter inputs
step.text: Enter dimensions into the Landscaping Cost Calculator and choose material/unit.

step.name: Add waste & price
step.text: Add waste percentage (5-10% rectangle, 10-15% complex) and optional price per unit.

step.name: Get results
step.text: Read volume, weight and cost instantly and copy/share results.

mainEntity.name: What does the Landscaping Cost Calculator calculate?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Landscaping Cost Calculator estimates landscaping cost quantity for US jobs — Paver count from area / paver area, Base gravel and sand volume, Mulch yards vs bags. Enter dimensions, choose units, add waste and price to get instant results.

mainEntity.name: How do I measure for landscaping cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Measure patio 12x10 ft =120 ft2, paver 12x12 in on site. Use the unit selectors — the tool converts inches→feet (÷12) and yards→feet (×3) before math. For non-rectangular, split into rectangles and add.

mainEntity.name: How much waste should I add?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add 10% for cuts and curves — 15% for radial patterns.

mainEntity.name: How accurate is this landscaping cost estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Math is exact for your inputs. Actual needs vary by site, material and installation. Add 5–10% waste for rectangular, 10–15% for irregular.

schemas.description: Calculate mulch in cubic yards and bags for garden beds & paths. Enter length, width, depth & areas — get yards, bags & cost with waste.

schemas.name: Mulch Calculator — Cubic Yards, Bags & Cost (2026)
schemas.description: Calculate mulch in cubic yards and bags for garden beds & paths. Enter length, width, depth & areas — get yards, bags & cost with waste.

mainEntity.name: How much mulch do I need for my beds?

acceptedAnswer.text: Measure each bed’s length, width and depth, then use the calculator. For one 20×10 ft bed at 3 inches, that’s 50 ft³ = 1.85 yd³. Set Number of areas for identical beds, or run the calculator per bed and sum. The result shows both cubic yards for bulk and bags for bagged mulch so you can compare.

mainEntity.name: How many cubic yards of mulch do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cubic yards = Length × Width × (Depth ÷ 12) × areas ÷ 27. Depth in inches is divided by 12 first. The calculator handles feet, inches, meters and yards — a 10×10 ft bed at 2 inches is 0.62 yd³, at 3 inches 0.93 yd³. Add waste after, not before.

mainEntity.name: How many bags of mulch do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bags = ceil(cubic feet with waste ÷ bag size). US bags are most commonly 2 ft³ (also 1.5 and 3 ft³). One 2-ft³ bag covers ~12 sq ft at 2 inches or ~8 sq ft at 3 inches. A 1.85-yd³ bed needs 25 bags of 2 ft³ (28 with 10% waste). Use Bulk for no bags and order by yards.

mainEntity.name: How deep should mulch be?

acceptedAnswer.text: Garden beds: 2–3 inches once settled. New beds: 3 inches initially to account for ~15% settling in the first weeks. Play areas: 3–4 inches, but check safety standards — deeper than 4 inches can stay too wet and suffocate roots. Don’t exceed 3 inches around tree trunks (keep a 6-inch clearance).

mainEntity.name: How much area does one yard of mulch cover?

acceptedAnswer.text: One cubic yard covers about 162 sq ft at 2 inches, 108 sq ft at 3 inches, 81 sq ft at 4 inches. The inverse: a 10×10 ft bed (100 sq ft) needs ~0.62 yd³ at 2 inches, ~0.93 yd³ at 3 inches. For paver borders next to beds, size the hardscape separately so mulch doesn’t mix.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert mulch bags to cubic yards?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bags × bag ft³ ÷ 27 = yards. Example: 10 bags of 2 ft³ = 20 ft³ ÷ 27 = 0.74 yd³. The calculator shows both instantly. If you’re comparing a bulk quote of $35 per yard to $4.50 per bag ($60 per yard equivalent at 13.5 bags per yard), bulk wins over ~5 yards.

mainEntity.name: How much does mulch cost per yard or per bag?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bulk mulch is often $25–$45 per yard plus delivery, bags $4–$7 per 2 ft³ in 2026. A 1.85-yd³ bed at $35 per yard is ~$65; the same as 28 bags at $4.50 is $126 — bulk is nearly half for larger beds. Enter your price per bag or per yard; the calculator multiplies waste-adjusted bags or yards for a material-only total.

schemas.name: Paver Calculator — Pavers, Base & Sand (2026)
schemas.description: Calculate pavers for patios & walkways. Enter area & paver size to get paver count, base gravel & sand in cubic yards with waste.

mainEntity.name: How many pavers do I need for my patio?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide area by paver area and round up, then add waste. Example: 12×12 inch paver = 1 ft², so a 200 sq ft patio needs 200 pavers before waste. A 4×8 inch paver is 0.222 ft², so the same patio needs 900 pavers (4.5 per ft²). Enter your paver length and width — the calculator does ceil(area ÷ (length × width)) and shows the waste-adjusted count.

mainEntity.name: How many pavers are needed per square foot?

acceptedAnswer.text: Count = 1 ÷ paver area in ft². Common: 12×12 = 1 per ft², 6×12 = 2 per ft², 4×8 = 4.5 per ft², 6×9 = 2.7 per ft². For running bond or herringbone, add 5% extra beyond the 10% rectangular waste because cuts increase. The calculator lets you test 12×12 vs 4×8 instantly.

mainEntity.name: How much paver base do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Patio on soil: 4 inches of compacted crushed base (6–8 inches for driveways). Base volume is area × depth ÷ 27 for cubic yards. For 200 sq ft at 4 inches, that’s 2.47 yd³ before waste, 2.72 yd³ with 10%. Order base as crusher run and size it with the Gravel Calculator if you need tons.

mainEntity.name: How much sand do I need for pavers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bedding sand is typically 1 inch (0.083 ft) of concrete sand screeded over the base. Sand yards = area × 0.083 ÷ 27. For 200 sq ft that’s 0.62 yd³, 0.68 yd³ with waste — about 1.5 tons of sand. Don’t use more than 1 inch; excess sand causes settling. Polymeric joint sand is extra and sold by the bag.

mainEntity.name: How much extra should I order for cuts and waste?

acceptedAnswer.text: 10% for a simple rectangle with saw cuts, 15% for curves, circles or diagonal layouts, and add another 5% for herringbone where every edge is a cut. The calculator’s waste multiplies pavers, base and sand together. Keep a few extra pavers after the job for future repairs — dye lots vary.

mainEntity.name: How do I handle odd shapes or multiple areas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Split the shape into rectangles, calculate each, and add the totals. The paver count is purely area-based, so an L-shape (e.g., 12×10 plus 8×6) is two runs. If you have a circular pad, use its diameter as length and width and the calculator will slightly overestimate — trim the waste to 10% instead of 15%.

mainEntity.name: How much does a paver patio cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pavers $3–$6 per sq ft, base gravel $30–$50 per ton, sand $20–$40 per yard, plus edging and polymeric sand. A 200 sq ft patio needs ~220 pavers, 2.7 yd³ base and 0.7 yd³ sand before delivery. Enter your paver price or leave it blank for a quantity-only plan, then compare to a poured concrete slab for the same footprint.

schemas.description: Calculate pea gravel in cubic yards and tons for patios & paths. Enter length, width & depth — get yards, tons & cost with waste instantly.

mainEntity.name: How much pea gravel do I need for a 10×10 patio?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 100 sq ft patio at 2 inches needs about 0.62 yd³ (≈0.83 tons or 34 bags of 50 lb), at 3 inches about 0.93 yd³ (≈1.25 tons). The calculator does Length × Width × (Depth ÷ 12) ÷ 27 for yards, then × 1.35 for tons, and adds waste. For driveways, use the Driveway Gravel Calculator which sizes base and top layers separately.

mainEntity.name: How much area does one ton of pea gravel cover?

acceptedAnswer.text: About 120 sq ft at 2 inches, 80 sq ft at 3 inches, 60 sq ft at 4 inches and 40 sq ft at 6 inches when using 1.35 tons per yard. Wet material covers slightly less. Compare to the general Gravel Calculator if you’re deciding between pea gravel and crushed stone — pea gravel is lighter and never compacts.

mainEntity.name: How deep should pea gravel be?

acceptedAnswer.text: Decorative beds: 2 inches. Walkways and patios: 2–3 inches over a compacted base with landscape fabric and edging. Dog runs and drainage beds: 3–4 inches. Playground safety surfacing: 9–12 inches per CPSC guidelines — at that depth pea gravel is often not preferred; check local codes. Going deeper than 4 inches feels unstable because rounded stone shifts underfoot.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert pea gravel cubic yards to tons?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply cubic yards by 1.35. One cubic yard is 27 ft³ or 54 bags of 0.5 ft³. One ton is 0.74 yd³ of pea gravel. The calculator shows ft³, yd³, tons and pounds together so you can compare a bag quote from a home store to a bulk ton quote instantly.

mainEntity.name: What’s the difference between pea gravel and crushed stone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pea gravel is rounded, smooth and loose — it drains well and stays decorative but never locks together. Crushed stone is angular and compacts to a firm surface, better for driveways and bases. For a firm patio base, size the lower lift with the Gravel Calculator using crushed stone, then top with pea gravel.

mainEntity.name: How much does pea gravel cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bulk pea gravel is typically $35–$60 per ton delivered, or $40–$65 per yard, plus $50–$150 delivery per load in 2026. Bags (0.5 ft³) are $4–$8 each — about $240–$480 per ton equivalent, so bulk wins over ~50 sq ft. Enter your price per yard or per ton; the calculator multiplies waste-adjusted yards or tons for a material-only total.

mainEntity.name: Do I need landscape fabric under pea gravel?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fabric helps suppress weeds and keeps stone from sinking into soil, but it can impede drainage in French drains. For patios and paths, use woven fabric with firm edging; for drainage layers, skip fabric or use non-woven geotextile as your engineer specifies. Add 10% waste for edge trimming regardless.

schemas.name: Roof Pitch Calculator — Ratio, Angle & Slope (2026)
schemas.description: Calculate roof pitch from rise and run — get pitch ratio, angle in degrees, slope & x:12. Enter rise & run in any units — instant results.

mainEntity.name: What is roof pitch and how is it measured?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pitch is rise over run — e.g., 6:12 means 6 inches of vertical rise per 12 inches of horizontal run. On site, level a 12-inch ruler horizontally from the roof surface and measure vertically to the rafter; that vertical is the pitch number. The calculator converts any units to a common base before dividing.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate roof pitch from rise and run?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide rise by run for decimal slope, then Angle = arctan(rise ÷ run) × 180/π. Example: 6 ÷ 12 = 0.50 slope → arctan(0.50) = 26.6°. Pitch per 12 is slope × 12, so 0.50 × 12 = 6:12. Enter any rise and run — the calculator shows ratio, angle, decimal slope and percent at once.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert roof pitch to degrees?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use degrees = arctan(rise ÷ run) × 57.2958. Common conversions: 4:12 = 18.4°, 6:12 = 26.6°, 8:12 = 33.7°, 12:12 = 45°. The tool handles this and also shows percent slope (rise/run × 100). For area, use the Roof Square Footage Calculator which needs pitch.

mainEntity.name: What does 4/12 or 6/12 roof pitch mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: It’s rise in inches per 12 inches of run. 4/12 rises 4 inches over a foot — low slope. 6/12 rises 6 inches — medium. 12/12 rises 12 inches — steep, 45°. Higher first numbers are steeper, shed water and snow faster, but need different underlayment and safety gear.

mainEntity.name: What is a common roof pitch for US homes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most US homes are 4:12 to 9:12. 4:12–6:12 is common for suburban gables, 6:12–8:12 for steeper traditional or snow country, below 3:12 is considered low-slope and often requires membrane roofing. Check manufacturer specs — many shingles require ≥2:12 with special underlayment and ≥4:12 for standard install.

mainEntity.name: How does roof pitch affect roof area and cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Steeper pitch increases true area vs footprint. A 6:12 pitch multiplies footprint by ~1.118 (√(6²+144)/12). So a 1,200 sq ft footprint becomes ~1,342 sq ft of roof. The Roof Square Footage Calculator applies this multiplier plus overhang and waste to get squares (1 square = 100 ft²).

mainEntity.name: What pitch should I choose for my climate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Low slope (<3:12) needs continuous membrane to prevent ponding. Moderate 4:12–6:12 balances cost and shedding. Steep >9:12 sheds snow best but costs more in material, labor and fall protection. In high-wind or hurricane zones, follow local code for fastening. Always confirm with your roofer and code official before ordering.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate roof square footage from building size?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with footprint including overhangs: (Length + 2×overhang) × (Width + 2×overhang) × sections. Multiply by the pitch multiplier √(pitch²+144) ÷ 12 to get true roof area. Divide by 100 for roofing squares. The calculator does this and adds waste last. Find your pitch first with the Roof Pitch Calculator if you don’t know it.

mainEntity.name: How many roofing squares do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: One square is 100 sq ft of roof area. After you get roof square footage, divide by 100. Example: 1,586 sq ft = 15.86 squares → order 17–18 squares with waste. Shingles are sold by the square or by bundles (typically 3 bundles per square for 3-tab, which varies by product). Always round up — partial squares aren’t sold.

mainEntity.name: Does roof pitch affect square footage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — steeper pitch means more area than the footprint. Multiplier examples: 4:12 = 1.054, 6:12 = 1.118, 8:12 = 1.202, 12:12 = 1.414. A 1,200 sq ft footprint at 6:12 is ~1,342 sq ft of roof. The calculator applies the multiplier automatically once you enter pitch.

mainEntity.name: Should I include roof overhang in the calculation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — add overhang to both length and width before multiplying. A 1.5-ft overhang on a 40×30 ft building makes footprint 43×33 ft. Overhang is added before the pitch multiplier, not after, because the sloped area includes the eave. If your overhang varies, measure each side separately and average.

mainEntity.name: How do I handle multiple sections, dormers or hips?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use Roof sections for identical gables (e.g., 2 for a main house plus garage). For dormers, calculate the main roof, then subtract large dormer footprints if they’re significant, or add 5% to area for hips and valleys which add cuts. The tool assumes a simple gable — add 5% for hips, 15% waste for complex roofs.

mainEntity.name: How much waste should I add for roofing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Simple gable with few penetrations: 10%. Hips, valleys, dormers or lots of valleys: 15%. Complex cuts, starter and ridge caps, and hip/ridge shingles are extra beyond field squares. The calculator’s waste control lets you test 10% vs 15% and see squares instantly.

mainEntity.name: What’s the difference between roof area and footprint?

acceptedAnswer.text: Footprint is the building’s ground projection. Roof area is larger because of slope and overhang. For example, a 40×30 ft building (1,200 ft² footprint) with 1.5-ft overhangs is 1,419 ft² footprint, then at 6:12 pitch it’s ~1,586 ft² roof. Use footprint for foundation, roof area for shingles.

mainEntity.name: What does the Slab Reinforcement Calculator calculate?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Slab Reinforcement Calculator estimates slab reinforcement quantity for US jobs — Slab area in square feet, Concrete volume in cubic yards, Bags and reinforcement with waste. Enter dimensions, choose units, add waste and price to get instant results.

mainEntity.name: How do I measure for slab reinforcement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Measure slab reinforcement 20 ft x 10 ft x 4 in on site. Use the unit selectors — the tool converts inches→feet (÷12) and yards→feet (×3) before math. For non-rectangular, split into rectangles and add.

acceptedAnswer.text: Add 5–10% for spillage and thickness variation — 10% safe for hand-screeded patios.

mainEntity.name: How accurate is this slab reinforcement estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Topsoil Cost Calculator estimates topsoil cost quantity for US jobs — Cubic yards and cubic feet, Tons and pounds using 1.35–1.60 t/yd³, Cost per ton or per yard with waste. Enter dimensions, choose units, add waste and price to get instant results.

mainEntity.name: How do I measure for topsoil cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Measure 3.67 tons @ $45/ton + $75 delivery on site. Use the unit selectors — the tool converts inches→feet (÷12) and yards→feet (×3) before math. For non-rectangular, split into rectangles and add.

mainEntity.name: How much waste should I add?

acceptedAnswer.text: Open-graded stone settles ~8% (×1.10), crusher run compacts 15–25% (×1.20). Add after volume.

mainEntity.name: How accurate is this topsoil cost estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Math is exact for your inputs. Actual needs vary by site, material and installation. Add 5–10% waste for rectangular, 10–15% for irregular.

acceptedAnswer.text: Math is exact for your inputs. Actual needs vary by site, material and installation. Add 5–10% waste for rectangular, 10–15% for irregular.
